meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I am a deeply superficial person'?
meta.ogDescription: Warhol's most-quoted paradox has no documented source — not in his books, not in any dated interview. Here's the paper trail.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Warhol’s most-quoted paradox has no documented origin. It is absent from his own books, and no speech, interview, letter or dated remark has ever been cited for it — the earliest printing we could locate is a 1984 quotation anthology that gives no source at all. It is thoroughly Warhol in spirit, and nobody else claims it, but the exact wording cannot be pinned to him.

source.heading: The paper trail

docMeta.dd: None located — no speech, book, interview or letter

source.excerpt: I am a deeply superficial person.
trail: The specialists have not ruled on it. A site search of Quote Investigator ↗ returns nothing, and Wikiquote’s Andy Warhol page ↗ does not carry the line in any section — not sourced, not disputed, not even unsourced.

A full-text search of Internet Archive’s scanned books ↗ returns roughly eighty printings of the phrase. The ones we opened are quotation anthologies, bathroom readers, astrology guides and books about Warhol quoting the anthologies — and none of them names a source. Warhol’s own books are in that same searchable corpus, and the line is not in them.

The earliest printing we could find is Robert Byrne, The Other 637 Best Things Anybody Ever Said (New York: Atheneum, 1984) ↗ — published while Warhol was alive, but in a book whose format gives no citations for anything.

Warhol is a documented magnet for words he never spoke. The Warhol Museum’s chief archivist Matt Wrbican showed in a 2007 essay, “The True Story of ‘My True Story’,” that most of the famous statements in Gretchen Berg’s 1 November 1966 East Village Other piece were Berg’s phrasing, not Warhol’s — the tape has him replying “Yeah” and “No” (Warholstars ↗).
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller context to give. Unlike a line lifted from a paragraph, this one has only ever appeared as a free-standing epigram — in Robert Byrne’s 1984 anthology it sits as bare entry 189, between a line about Prince Sihanouk and one beginning “I have bursts…”, with nothing but the name “Andy Warhol” beneath it.

source.rightsNote: Because the wording cannot be tied to any published work, no copyright status can honestly be asserted. If Warhol said it, the words would belong to his estate; if the sentence was shaped by an editor or anthologist, rights would follow that publication instead. Either way, an American source from the 1960s onward would be in copyright, not public domain — so this line should never be treated as free to reuse.

author.name: Andy Warhol
author.heading: About Andy Warhol
author.bio: Born Andrew Warhola Jr. in Pittsburgh in 1928, Warhol turned commercial illustration into the central language of American art — soup cans, Marilyns, electric chairs — and then turned himself into the work. Through the Factory he made films, managed the Velvet Underground, founded Interview magazine and cultivated a public self so flat and evasive that critics have argued for decades about whether anything lay behind it. He died in New York in 1987 after routine gallbladder surgery, leaving behind books, diaries, hundreds of hours of tape — and a great many famous sentences that cannot be traced to any of them.

misattribution.heading: What’s actually wrong here
misattribution.intro: Nobody else claims this sentence, and no researcher has debunked it. The problem is narrower and more stubborn: it is a famous quotation with no origin, riding on a name that has a proven history of being handed words its owner never said.

items.why: Neither Quote Investigator ↗ nor Wikiquote ↗ carries it, and the printings we opened in Internet Archive’s scanned books ↗ are quotation anthologies repeating it without a citation.
The Quotations Page ↗ — one of the earliest online quote databases — lists it with nothing but Warhol’s life dates, crediting it to a compiler’s personal collection rather than to any Warhol text.

items.scope: The precedent that should worry you
items.why: Warhol’s single most-quoted line — “If you want to know all about Andy Warhol, just look at the surface…” — was shown by Warhol Museum archivist Matt Wrbican in 2007 to be his interviewer’s composition, not his (Warholstars ↗). An unsourced Warhol aphorism deserves more scepticism than an unsourced aphorism from almost anyone else.

misattribution.truthLine: Best honest verdict: widely credited to Warhol, perfectly in character, printed during his lifetime — and still, forty years on, without a single documented source ↗.

context.heading: Why this one is so hard to pin down
lead: Warhol built a career out of refusing to be the author of his own statements. He sent a lookalike on a lecture tour, answered interviewers in monosyllables, let assistants make his art and let editors make his sentences. A line that says I am a deeply superficial person is therefore both perfectly in character and almost impossible to verify — the persona was designed to leave no fingerprints.

The sentence works because it collapses in on itself: “deeply” is the word you use for a soul, “superficial” the word you use for its absence. Warhol’s whole project ran on that short circuit. Which is exactly why it is so easy to believe — and why belief is not evidence.
detailsBody: An observation worth flagging, though it proves nothing on its own: two Warhol biographies — Jan Greenberg and Sandra Jordan’s Andy Warhol: Prince of Pop and Tony Scherman and David Dalton’s Pop: The Genius of Andy Warhol — record a near-identical line as a habitual saying ↗: “I’m deeply superficial.” Greenberg and Jordan give it not to Warhol but to Fred Hughes, his business manager — “‘I’m deeply superficial,’ Fred often said.” Neither book claims Hughes coined it, and it is at least as likely he was quoting his employer. But it is a reminder that the phrase was in the air around the Factory, and that lines travelled freely in that room.

The oldest printing we could find sits in a 1984 anthology whose entries carry no citations by design. That is the shape of the whole trail: anthologies copying anthologies, then websites copying anthologies. At no point does the chain touch a tape, a transcript, a page or a date.
context.pull: A quotation that sounds like the person is the hardest kind to check.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Andy Warhol page contains no entry for 'deeply superficial' in any section (sourced, disputed or unsourced).
Quote Investigator has no article on 'deeply superficial' — a site search returns 'Nothing Found'.

Full-text search of Internet Archive's scanned books returns ~83 printings of 'a deeply superficial person' (the narrower query 'I am a deeply superficial person' returns ~48); the printings opened are quotation anthologies and none of them cites a source; the earliest is the 1984 Byrne anthology, and Warhol's own books (which are in the same searchable corpus) do not appear.
The Other 637 Best Things Anybody Ever Said is by Robert Byrne, published by Atheneum, New York, in 1984.

Warhol Museum chief archivist Matt Wrbican showed in a 2007 essay, 'The True Story of My True Story', that most of the statements in Gretchen Berg's 1 November 1966 East Village Other interview were Berg's words rather than Warhol's; the transcript shows Warhol answering 'Well, I like - I guess, yeah', 'The surface', 'Yeah' and 'No'.

The Quotations Page lists 'I am a deeply superficial person' under Andy Warhol with only his life dates (US artist, 1928-1987), crediting it to 'Michael Moncur's (Cynical) Quotations' and giving no original source.
The Muscarelle Museum of Art's exhibition page states 'Warhol, fascinated by contradictions, famously said, I am a deeply superficial person' without giving a source.
Andy Warhol was born Andrew Warhola Jr. on 6 August 1928 in Pittsburgh and died 22 February 1987; The Philosophy of Andy Warhol was published in 1975 and POPism in 1980.
The Philosophy of Andy Warhol: From A to B and Back Again is held and scanned by the Internet Archive (and is therefore inside the full-text corpus searched above).

Full-text search for "I'm deeply superficial" returns 13 hits, including Jan Greenberg & Sandra Jordan, Andy Warhol: Prince of Pop ("'I'm deeply superficial,' Fred often said, boasting that he had memorized the names...") and Tony Scherman & David Dalton, Pop: The Genius of Andy Warhol / Andy Warhol: His Controversial Life, Art and Colourful Times ("'I'm deeply superficial,' he liked to say").
